Describe the feature clearly here. Be sure to convey here why the requested feature is needed. Any brief description about the use-case would help.
Luong-style attention attention use three types of scoring methods, namely dot, general and concat. This can be found in the 3rd page of the [original paper](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1508.04025.pdf) and explained [here](https://stackoverflow.com/a/44454253). 
![tiQkz](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/56781123/148428296-f88efa8d-5d59-4099-9ee1-cca4410385c4.png)

Right now `concat` method for scoring is not implemented and only [dot and general](https://github.com/keras-team/keras/blob/master/keras/layers/dense_attention.py#L339) has been implemented in the layer. An use case can be found [here](https://github.com/spro/practical-pytorch/blob/master/seq2seq-translation/seq2seq-translation.ipynb). 


**Will this change the current api? How?**
Yes. An extra parameter in the Attention layer to specify the scoring method. 

**Who will benefit from this feature?**
Anyone using Luong-style attention layer can opt for concat scoring method.

messages.claude:
feat: Add concat score_mode to Attention layer

Add a new `score_mode` parameter to `keras.layers.Attention` to support the "concat" scoring method used in Luong-style attention, complementing the existing "dot" mode.

Issue #15866 highlights that Luong-style attention defines three scoring functions (dot, general, concat), but only the dot product was implemented in the Attention layer. This prevented users from selecting the concat-based score, which computes attention via the hyperbolic tangent of the sum (broadcast) of query and key vectors, weighted by a trainable `concat_score_weight` parameter. The concat formulation is useful in seq2seq and translation models where dot-product scoring may be unsuitable due to vector dimensionality or representational considerations.

Implementation details:
- Introduce `score_mode` argument (default 'dot') to `Attention.__init__`, with validation restricting it to {'dot', 'concat'}.
- In `build`, create a trainable scalar `concat_score_weight` (initialized to ones) when score_mode == 'concat'; otherwise it is None.
- In `_calculate_scores`, branch on score_mode: 'dot' retains the existing matmul (and optional scale) path; 'concat' reshapes query/key for broadcasting, optionally applies the scale, applies tanh, reduces sum over the last axis, and multiplies by `concat_score_weight`.
- Serialize `score_mode` in `get_config` so layers round-trip correctly.
- Add unit tests covering multi-dim concat scoring, one-dim concat scoring with scale, and shape validation (with and without an explicit key) for the concat path.

This unblocks anyone needing Luong-style concat attention without a custom layer, and aligns the Keras Attention layer with the scoring options described in the original attention paper.
messages.kimi:
feat: Add concat score_mode to Attention layer for Luong-style attention

Add support for the "concat" scoring method in the Attention layer, complementing the existing "dot" method. This implements the concat scoring function from the Luong attention paper (arXiv:1508.04025), which computes scores as v^T * tanh(W_q * q + W_k * k).

The implementation:
- Adds `score_mode` parameter accepting "dot" (default) or "concat"
- Creates `concat_score_weight` trainable variable when score_mode="concat"
- Computes concat scores using tanh of query+key with learned weight
- Maintains backward compatibility with existing dot product behavior
- Includes comprehensive unit tests for multi-dim and scale scenarios

This addresses issue #15866, allowing users to choose between dot and concat attention scoring methods for Luong-style attention layers.
messages.minimax:
feat: Add concat scoring mode to Attention layer

Implement Luong-style concat attention scoring method in keras.layers.Attention.

The Attention layer previously only supported 'dot' scoring (Luong-style also
supports 'concat' scoring per the original paper). This change adds the
'score_mode' parameter to enable concat scoring, which uses tanh of the
concatenated query and key vectors instead of dot product.

- Add score_mode parameter ('dot' or 'concat') with validation
- Add concat_score_weight trainable weight for concat scoring
- Update _calculate_scores to compute tanh-based concatenation scores
- Update get_config to serialize score_mode for checkpointing
- Add comprehensive tests for concat scoring mode

messages.kimi:
fix: Correct EfficientNetV2 survival_probability calculation by incrementing block counter

The survival_probability for stochastic depth was incorrectly calculated because the block counter `b` was never incremented, causing all blocks to use `drop_connect_rate * 0 / blocks` instead of progressively increasing values. This fix increments `b` after each block is processed, matching the reference Google implementation where survival probability increases with block depth.
messages.claude:
fix: increment block counter in EfficientNetV2 drop connect rate

The `b` variable used to compute `survival_probability` in the MBConv blocks
was never incremented, leaving it stuck at zero for every block. This caused
the drop connect rate to be effectively disabled across the entire network,
which diverges from the reference Google implementation where the survival
probability decreases as the block index increases (i.e., deeper blocks
experience more dropout).

The fix adds `b += 1` after each block is constructed so that
`survival_probability = drop_connect_rate * b / blocks` ramps up correctly
from shallow to deep blocks, matching the upstream behavior described in
issue #16144.
messages.minimax:
fix: increment block counter for correct survival_probability calculation in EfficientNetV2

The block counter `b` was never incremented inside the loop, causing `survival_probability` to always be computed as `drop_connect_rate * 0 / blocks = 0` instead of scaling with block index as in the Google implementation. This caused EfficientNetV2 to not match the reference implementation's behavior regarding stochastic depth drop connect rates.

fix: Correct misuse of assertTrue in loss_scale_optimizer_test.py

Remove incorrect second argument (4.) from assertTrue call in testSerializationWithBuiltInOptimizer. The test was incorrectly passing assertTrue with two arguments, where the second argument was being interpreted as a message rather than a comparison value. This fixes the test to properly verify opt.dynamic is True without the erroneous extra argument, aligning with the intended test behavior described in #16072.
messages.claude:
fix: remove misused second argument in assertTrue call

The test `testSerializationWithBuiltInOptimizer` was calling
`self.assertTrue(opt.dynamic, 4.)`, which is a misuse of
`assertTrue`. `assertTrue` evaluates only the truthiness of its
first argument; any additional positional arguments are treated as
the assertion message, not as comparison targets. As a result the
`4.` was silently ignored, and the assertion would pass for any
truthy value of `opt.dynamic` rather than verifying the intended
value.

Per issue #16072, several tests across the codebase misuse
`assertTrue` for comparisons that should use `assertEqual`. In this
specific case the second argument was not a meaningful comparison
target — `opt.dynamic` is a boolean — so the correct fix is to drop
the stray `4.` argument entirely, leaving a plain truthiness check.
messages.minimax:
Fix assertTrue misuse in loss_scale_optimizer_test

assertTrue takes only a condition argument, not a comparison value.
The test was incorrectly passing `opt.dynamic` and `4.` as two
separate arguments, causing it to pass whenever `opt.dynamic` was
truthy rather than actually comparing the value to `4.`. Changed to
pass only the boolean condition `opt.dynamic`.

messages.claude:
fix: resolve ThresholdedReLU crash on list input by using compute_dtype

ThresholdedReLU.call() previously cast self.theta to inputs.dtype and
relied on inputs.dtype directly. When a list of tensors was passed in
(as opposed to a single Tensor), inputs had no .dtype attribute, raising
AttributeError and crashing the layer. ReLU and LeakyReLU already accept
list inputs because they delegate to the backend implementation.

Replace inputs.dtype with self.compute_dtype (the layer's compute dtype,
which is well-defined regardless of whether inputs is a Tensor or a list)
and cast self.theta through that same dtype. This brings ThresholdedReLU
in line with the behavior of the other activation layers and resolves
issue #16273, where passing a list of tensors to ThresholdedReLU failed
with "'list' object has no attribute 'dtype'".
messages.kimi:
fix: Fix ThresholdedReLU crash when input is a list

The ThresholdedReLU layer was crashing with AttributeError when receiving list inputs because it directly accessed `inputs.dtype`, which doesn't exist for Python lists. Unlike ReLU and LeakyReLU which use backend implementations that handle list inputs properly, ThresholdedReLU implemented its own call method that assumed tensor inputs.

Changed to use `self.compute_dtype` instead of `inputs.dtype` for casting operations, consistent with how other activation layers handle dtype resolution. This allows ThresholdedReLU to accept list inputs like other Keras activation layers, fixing the inconsistency reported in issue #16273.
messages.minimax:
fix ThresholdedReLU crash when input is a list by using self.compute_dtype

When inputs is a Python list rather than a tensor, accessing inputs.dtype raises an AttributeError since lists have no dtype attribute. The fix uses self.compute_dtype instead, which is the layer's computed dtype property that does not depend on the input being a tensor. This matches the pattern used by similar layers like ReLU that handle list inputs correctly.

The vocabulary_size() method in IndexLookup layer was calling .numpy() on the lookup table size, which fails in graph mode when eager execution is disabled. This change adds a check for tf.executing_eagerly() to conditionally use .numpy() only when in eager mode, allowing the method to work correctly in both eager and graph execution contexts. messages.claude:
fix: make vocabulary_size() work in graph mode

The vocabulary_size() method of preprocessing layers (e.g., StringLookup)
called .numpy() on the lookup table size, which only works in eager mode.
Calling it inside a graph context (e.g., within tf.function) raised an
exception, leaving users unable to retrieve the vocabulary size in graph mode.

Fix by branching on tf.executing_eagerly(): in eager mode keep the original
behavior returning a Python int, while in graph mode return the tf.Tensor
result of lookup_table.size() + _token_start_index(), which is symbolically
traceable and matches the expected behavior described in issue #16453.

messages.kimi:
fix: Add tf.Tensor to ARRAY_TYPES for validation_split support with TF backend

Add `tf.Tensor` to `ARRAY_TYPES` in `data_adapter_utils.py` to fix `model.fit()` failure when using `validation_split` with TensorFlow backend. The issue occurred because `np.ndarray` was incorrectly included instead of `tf.Tensor` in the TensorFlow backend check, causing valid TensorFlow tensors to be rejected during validation split processing.

Also fix the error message formatting by adding the missing f-string prefix for the `{unsplitable}` variable, and add comprehensive test coverage for `validation_split` functionality across eager, graph, and JIT compilation modes.
messages.claude:
fix: support tf.Tensor in validation_split and fix unsplitable variable formatting

When using keras_core with the TF backend, model.fit() fails to train
when provided with validation_split, while it works fine without it.
The root cause is that tf.Tensor was missing from ARRAY_TYPES in
data_adapter_utils.py, so any input given as a tf.Tensor (e.g. the
output of tf.one_hot) was rejected as an incompatible type for
validation_split.

- Fixed the error message in _can_split: the {unsplitable} placeholder

messages.claude:
fix: wrap LSTM/GRU in tf.function to fix masking layer on GPU (#18397)

Decorating keras.backend.tensorflow.rnn.gru, lstm, and _cudnn_lstm with
@tf.function (autograph=False for _cudnn_lstm) ensures the graph is
traced properly when running on GPU.

Why: when a Masking layer is used together with an LSTM on the TF backend
with a GPU, training fails with "Using a symbolic tf.Tensor as a Python
bool is not allowed: AutoGraph is disabled in this function." The mask
propagation path relies on the function being traced as a tf.function,
so wrapping the RNN entry points enables the symbolic mask tensor to be
handled correctly and unblocks GPU training of masked LSTM/GRU models.

messages.kimi:
feat: Add `median` and `quantile` operations to all backends

Implement `median` and `quantile` operations across JAX, NumPy, TensorFlow, and Torch backends. These are important statistical functions available in PyTorch and JAX that were missing from Keras ops. The implementation includes proper dtype handling (casting int64 to floatx), support for multiple axes, all quantile methods (linear, lower, higher, midpoint, nearest), and workarounds for JAX's keepdims bug when axis=None. This addresses the feature request in issue #18409 for adding Median to keras_core.ops.
messages.minimax:
Add `quantile` and `median` to keras.ops.numpy

- Add `median` and `quantile` functions across all backends (JAX, NumPy, TensorFlow, Torch)
- These were requested in issue #18409 as missing numpy operations
- `median` computes the median along specified axes; `quantile` computes q-th quantiles with support for multiple interpolation methods (`linear`, `lower`, `higher`, `midpoint`, `nearest`)
- Both support `axis`, `keepdims` parameters; `quantile` additionally supports the `method` parameter for interpolation
- Handle edge cases like `axis=None` with `keepdims=True` which some backends don't natively support
messages.claude:
feat: add `median` and `quantile` ops across all backends

Add `median` and `quantile` operations to the Keras ops API, with
implementations for the JAX, NumPy, TensorFlow, and Torch backends.

Issue #18409 requested a `median` function in `keras_core.ops`, noting
that it is a commonly used statistic available in both `torch` and
`jax.numpy` but missing from Keras. `quantile` is added alongside it so
that median can be expressed as the 0.5-quantile (the TF backend delegates
to `quantile` directly), and because both share the same reduction
semantics (axis, keepdims, multi-axis support, and interpolation methods).

Backend-specific handling is required because the underlying libraries
differ in coverage and behavior:
- The TensorFlow backend has no native `tf.quantile`, so a custom
  `_quantile` implementation (adapted from `tfp.stats.percentile`) is
  added, supporting `linear`, `lower`, `higher`, `midpoint`, and
  `nearest` methods plus NaN propagation.
- JAX's `jnp.median`/`jnp.quantile` do not honor `keepdims` when
  `axis=None`; this is worked around with an explicit `expand_dims` loop.
- `int64` inputs are cast to `config.floatx()` (matching NumPy's
  upcasting to float) and `bool` inputs are cast for backends that reject
  them (NumPy, Torch).
- For Torch, multiple axes are supported by transposing and reshaping
  into a single reduction axis, since `torch.quantile` only accepts a
  single dim.

Also adds `Median`/`Quantile` `Operation` classes for symbolic tracing,
registers both ops in `keras.ops.numpy`, and adds corresponding shape
and correctness tests.

context.issue:
Issue #18657: Use the `padding` arg when possible for torch backend
To support `padding="same"`, we implemented a custom padding by calling `torch.nn.functional.pad` for ops including `conv`, `max_pool`, and `average_pool`.

However, it takes more memory and slows down the model.

Torch does support some cases of `padding="same"`.
We should only use this manuall padding method when the native ops in torch doesn't support it.

messages.kimi:
perf: Optimize torch backend padding by using native padding arg when possible

Refactor `_apply_same_padding` in `keras/backend/torch/nn.py` to return the padding value instead of always applying manual padding. When padding is symmetric, pass the padding value directly to torch functions (max_pool1d/2d/3d, conv) via their native `padding` argument instead of calling `tnn.pad`. This reduces memory usage and improves performance by avoiding unnecessary tensor copying. Manual padding is now only applied when torch doesn't natively support the padding configuration (e.g., asymmetric padding or strided conv with dilation). Also removes unused `numpy` import and simplifies padding calculation logic.
messages.minimax:
performance: avoid unnecessary torch.pad calls in pooling and conv ops

When padding="same", the previous implementation always called torch.nn.functional.pad
which is slower and uses more memory. Torch natively supports padding in max_pool1d/2d/3d
and avg_pool1d/2d/3d for many cases. This change passes the padding argument directly to
the torch pooling functions when possible, only falling back to manual padding when necessary.

Fixes #18657
messages.claude:
perf: avoid calling pad() when possible for torch backend

* Refactor `_compute_padding_length` to drop the `numpy` dependency and
  use integer floor/ceil division directly on `total_padding_length`.
* Refactor `_apply_same_padding` to return a tuple of `(tensor, padding)`
  instead of always padding the input. When the padding is symmetric
  across all spatial dims, return the original tensor plus a padding
  value that can be passed to the native torch ops, avoiding an
  unnecessary `tnn.pad` call that hurts memory and performance.
* Update `max_pool`, `average_pool`, and `conv` call sites to thread the
  computed `padding` value through to `torch.nn.functional.max_pool{1,2,3}d`.
  For `average_pool`, guard the manual `tnn.pad` so it only runs when
  `uneven_padding` is non-empty.

Why: implementing `padding="same"` via `torch.nn.functional.pad` always
allocates a padded copy of the input, which is more expensive in both
memory and time than letting the native torch pooling/conv ops handle
the padding internally via their `padding` argument. Torch already
supports symmetric "same" padding natively; the manual `pad()` path is
only needed when the padding is asymmetric. This change keeps the manual
path as a fallback for the asymmetric case while routing the symmetric
case through the native `padding` arg, reducing memory usage and
improving throughput for `conv`, `max_pool`, and `average_pool` on the
torch backend. See issue #18657.

messages.kimi:
perf: Optimize LSTM/GRU performance by removing input validation from tf.function

Remove `_do_rnn_inputs_support_cudnn` function and inline simplified mask check to avoid expensive validation operations inside tf.function-decorated functions. The mask validation logic was causing significant overhead during model training, particularly for models with Bidirectional LSTM layers as reported in issue #18854 where steps per epoch took much longer in Keras 3.0 compared to keras_core. By removing the @tf.function decorator from gru() and lstm() functions and simplifying the mask check to a direct `mask is not None` comparison, we eliminate unnecessary graph operations that were slowing down execution. This aligns with the pattern established in previous performance fixes where input validation checks were moved outside tf.function-wrapped code paths to reduce compilation overhead.
messages.claude:
fix: remove redundant input support check and tf.function wrappers from LSTM/GRU to fix execution time regression

What:
- Remove `_do_rnn_inputs_support_cudnn` helper and its calls in `gru` and `lstm`;
  replace the guard with a direct `mask is not None` check.
- Drop the `@tf.function` decorator from `gru`, `lstm`, `_cudnn_gru`, and
  `_cudnn_lstm` (and the `@tf.function(autograph=False)` on the cudnn helpers).

Why:
Issue #18854 reports that `model.fit` runs dramatically slower on Keras 3
than on keras-core for bidirectional LSTM models, making training impractical.
The root cause is the input-support check (`_do_rnn_inputs_support_cudnn`)
being executed eagerly inside `gru`/`lstm` on every step. That helper builds
extra ops (`tf.reduce_all`, `tf.transpose`, `tf.logical_and`,
`_is_sequence_right_padded`, `_has_fully_masked_sequence`) solely to decide
whether the CuDNN path is allowed — work that should not run per step. By the
time execution reaches `gru`/`lstm`, the caller has already validated that
the CuDNN path is applicable, so re-checking the mask is redundant. The
equivalent check already lives in the public `rnn`/RNN layer, so the guard
here only rejects a valid case it should accept.

Removing the per-step `@tf.function` wrappers resolves the overhead from
retracing/compiling the function boundary on each invocation, which is the
primary source of the slowdown observed in the issue. The RNN layer itself
is already wrapped in a `tf.function` at the training step level, so the
inner decorators added no benefit and instead caused repeated graph work.

Falling back from `not inputs_supported` to `mask is not None` preserves
the original intent (block the CuDNN path when masking is used, since CuDNN
RNN ops do not support masking) while eliminating the eager mask analysis.
This restores training throughput comparable to keras-core for the
bidirectional-LSTM workload reported in #18854.

Remove the complex `_do_rnn_inputs_support_cudnn` check and `@tf.function` decorators from LSTM/GRU to improve training performance. The previous mask validation logic was overly restrictive and prevented CuDNN acceleration in valid use cases, causing significant slowdowns in `model.fit` when using masked recurrent layers.

messages.kimi:
fix: Preserve static shape in TensorFlow RNN when time steps are known at build time

This change ensures that when the number of time steps is fixed and known at build time, the static shape is propagated instead of being replaced with a dynamic shape from `tf.shape()`. This fixes an issue where `TimeDistributed` layers combined with RNN layers would fail with `Invalid dtype: <class 'NoneType'>` errors during graph execution, as the dynamic shape was causing shape inference to lose the static time dimension information.
messages.minimax:
Fix #18941: Allow static shape propagation in RNNs when time steps is known

When time_steps is fixed and known at build time, use the static value directly instead of calling tf.shape(), which prevents ValueError when using TimeDistributed with LSTM layers.
messages.claude:
fix: propagate static time steps shape in RNN swap_batch_timestep

Use the static time steps value when available instead of always falling
back to a dynamic tensor. Previously swap_batch_timestep unconditionally
called tf.shape(flattened_inputs[0])[0], which produced a symbolic tensor
even when the number of time steps was statically known. That dropped the
static shape information, so downstream layers (e.g. TimeDistributed
wrapping an LSTM with return_sequences=True) received an input whose
time dimension was None at build time and failed with "Invalid dtype:
<class 'NoneType'>" when fitting the model in graph mode.

Issue #18941 reports that TimeDistributed + LSTM raises
ValueError: Invalid dtype: <class 'NoneType'> during model.fit, while
working fine in eager mode. The root cause is that the static time-step
shape was not being propagated through the RNN, leaving downstream layers
to infer a None dimension. By preferring the static shape
(time_steps) and only using the dynamic tensor when it is None, the
static shape now flows through and the model builds and trains correctly
in graph mode.

Add `name` parameter to the `__init__` of all op classes. (#21376)

Follow up of https://github.com/keras-team/keras/pull/21373

This is to solve an inconsistency in the saving / reloading of ops. Some ops behave differently.

Consider this code:

```python
input = keras.layers.Input(shape=(4,), dtype="float32")
output = keras.ops.abs(input)
model = keras.models.Model(input, output)

json = model.to_json()
reloaded_model = keras.models.model_from_json(json)
reloaded_json = reloaded_model.to_json()
```

The reloaded model JSON is the same as the original model JSON. The `abs` op is serialized as

- `{"module": "keras.src.ops.numpy", "class_name": "Absolute", "config": {"name": "absolute"}, "registered_name": "Absolute", "name": "absolute", ...}`

Consider the same code with `abs` replaced with `sum`:

```python
input = keras.layers.Input(shape=(4,), dtype="float32")
output = keras.ops.abs(input)
model = keras.models.Model(input, output)

json = model.to_json()
reloaded_model = keras.models.model_from_json(json)
reloaded_json = reloaded_model.to_json()
```

The reloaded model JSON is different from the original JSON.

- `{"module": "keras.src.ops.numpy", "class_name": "Sum", "config": {"axis": null, "keepdims": false}, "registered_name": "Sum", "name": "sum", ...}`
- `{"module": "keras.src.ops.numpy", "class_name": "Sum", "config": {"axis": null, "keepdims": false}, "registered_name": "Sum", "name": "sum_1", ...}`

The reloaded `sum` op now has a name `"sum_1"` instead of `"sum"`.

This is because:
- `Abs` does not define `__init__` and inherits the `Operation.__init__` that has a `name` parameter.
- `Sum` defines `__init__` without a `name` parameter.

We want saving / reloading to be idempotent. Even though users cannot control the name of ops (although it would be easy to add), the auto-assigned names should be saved and reloaded. For this, `name` has to be supported in `__init__`.

This PR adds a `name` parameter to all existing `__init__` of op classes, which is passed to `super().__init__()`. Note that it is defined as a keyword only argument for forward compatibility in case more parameters get added in the feature.

Empty `__init__`s were removed.

Fix `UnravelIndex.__init__` which was not calling `super().__init__()`.

Issue #18976: chore: override item removal methods in tracking
Based on the TODO comments in keras/keras/utils/tracking.py

messages.kimi:
feat: implement item removal methods for TrackedList, TrackedDict, and TrackedSet

Implement `pop()`, `clear()`, `__delitem__()` for TrackedList, `pop()`, `popitem()`, `clear()` for TrackedDict, and `pop()`, `clear()` for TrackedSet. These methods properly untrack values before removal, ensuring consistent tracking behavior across all collection types. This resolves the TODO comments in tracking.py and prevents memory leaks when items are removed from tracked collections.
messages.claude:
feat: override remaining item removal methods in TrackedList, TrackedDict, and TrackedSet

The tracking module in keras/utils/tracking.py previously had TODO comments
on TrackedList, TrackedDict, and TrackedSet noting that item removal
methods were not yet overridden. Only `remove`/`discard` were
implemented, so removing items via other mutating paths (`pop`,
`popitem`, `clear`, `__delitem__`) silently bypassed the tracker. This
left stale references to variables and other tracked objects in the
tracker store, causing the tracked-variables collection to grow
unbounded and hold onto objects that were no longer reachable from the
container — leading to subtle memory leaks and incorrect results for
code that relies on the tracker to enumerate live variables (e.g. saved
model serialization).

This change implements the remaining removal entry points for each
container so that every removal path calls `tracker.untrack()` on the
evicted value(s):

- TrackedList: `pop`, `clear`, `__delitem__`
- TrackedDict: `pop`, `popitem`, `clear`
- TrackedSet: `pop`, `clear`

`__delitem__` retrieves the value before delegating to the parent
implementation so the value is still available to untrack. The dict
`pop` path guards against untracking the sentinel `default` when the
key is absent, and `popitem` untracks the popped value.

The corresponding TODO comments are removed.

Tests in tracking_test.py are extended to cover `pop`, `clear`, and
`__delitem__` on TrackedList, including cases where non-Variable entries
(such as `None` and `0`) are interleaved with tracked values, ensuring
the tracker count remains accurate and only real tracked objects affect
the count.

Addresses issue #18976.

feat: add keras.ops.linalg module with linear algebra operations across all backends

Add a unified linear algebra API in `keras.ops.linalg` exposing cholesky, det, eig, inv, lu_factor, norm, qr, solve, solve_triangular, and svd as Keras ops. Implement the corresponding backend primitives for the JAX, NumPy, TensorFlow, and Torch backends, and wire up the new `linalg` submodule in each backend's `__init__` plus the top-level `keras.ops` namespace.

Why: Issue #19062 reported that Keras 3 lacked equivalents for common `tf.linalg` operations (e.g. `eigh`, `solve`, `qr`, `norm`), forcing users to drop down to backend-specific APIs. By providing a single, backend-agnostic `keras.ops.linalg` surface, ops can be authored once and dispatched to the active backend, matching the multi-backend design goal of Keras 3. The implementations standardize behaviors that differ across backends — such as Cholesky failure detection (raising on NaNs for jax/tf), `lu_factor` pivot conventions (converting torch's 1-based pivots to 0-based), `norm` dtype promotion for integer inputs, `qr` mode validation, `solve`/`solve_triangular` rank normalization for 1-D `b`, and `svd` return-order unification (returning `u, s, vh`). Corresponding math-backend tests for `qr`, `solve`, and `norm` are removed in favor of dedicated linalg test coverage.

This addresses issue #19062 by providing Keras3 equivalents to tf.linalg operations. The linalg operations are migrated from `keras.ops.math` into a dedicated module, with corresponding backend implementations following the existing backend pattern.
messages.kimi:
feat: Add linear algebra operations module `keras.ops.linalg` (#19062)

This commit introduces a new `keras.ops.linalg` module that provides a unified linear algebra API across all Keras backends (JAX, NumPy, TensorFlow, and PyTorch). The implementation addresses the gap identified in issue #19062, where users needed replacements for `tf.linalg` operations.

The new module includes the following operations: `cholesky`, `det`, `eig`, `inv`, `lu_factor`, `norm`, `qr`, `solve`, `solve_triangular`, and `svd`. Each operation is implemented with backend-specific optimizations while maintaining a consistent API surface.

Key implementation details:
- JAX backend uses `jax.numpy.linalg` and `jax.scipy.linalg` with proper NaN handling for Cholesky decomposition

Issue #19180: `ValueError`: `ngrams` when loading a model with a `TextVectorization` layer
### Describe a bug

Loading a model that contains a `TextVectorization` layer with `ngram` set to a tuple results in a `ValueError`.

### Code to Reproduce

```python
import numpy as np
import tensorflow as tf
from tensorflow import keras

texts = np.array(['foo bar', 'bar baz', 'baz bada boom'])

model = keras.Sequential([
    keras.layers.Input(dtype=tf.string, shape=(1,)),
    keras.layers.TextVectorization(ngrams=(1, 2)),
])

model.layers[0].adapt(texts)
model(texts)
```
```text
<tf.Tensor: shape=(3, 5), dtype=int64, numpy=
array([[ 5,  3,  4,  0,  0],
       [ 3,  2,  8,  0,  0],
       [ 2, 10,  6,  7,  9]])>
```
```python
model.save('model.keras')
model = tf.keras.models.load_model('model.keras')  # raises `ValueError`
```
```text
ValueError: `ngrams` must be None, an integer, or a tuple of integers. Received: ngrams=[1, 2]
```

### Expected Results

The model is loaded. No error is raised.

### Actual Results

`ValueError` is raised.

### Cause and Possible Solutions

The error is raised in `__init__` method of `TextVectorization` class in [`text_vectorisation.py`](https://github.com/keras-team/keras/blob/02c1a4118a51be1bd076324fb4849e7353ee2544/keras/layers/preprocessing/text_vectorization.py#L283-L288). Perhaps, checking if the `ngram` parameter is a list and, if so, coercing it to a tuple would be a viable solution in this case.

### Versions
`Python 3.11.4`

```text
tensorflow == 2.14.1
tensorflow-metal == 1.1.0
```

messages.claude:
fix(preprocessing): resolve `ValueError` for `ngrams` tuple in TextVectorization

Coerce `ngrams` from a list back to a tuple during deserialization in

`TextVectorization` layer with `ngrams` set to a tuple (e.g. `(1, 2)`)

Received: ngrams=[1, 2]`.

deserialized config matches what the constructor expects, restoring
save/load compatibility for models that rely on n-gram extraction.

the tensorflow backend since it requires string input dtype.

Closes #19180.

messages.claude:
docs: add security awareness guidance to SECURITY.md (#19213)

Add a "Using Keras Securely" section to the Security Policy to inform
users of common security practices they should consider when running
models built with Keras.

The new content covers:
- Untrusted inputs: sandboxes, pre-analysis, updates, and input
  sanitation (validation, filtering, encoding, verification) to mitigate
  script/prompt injection risks.
- Data privacy: sandboxing model execution and testing for sensitive
  data leaks when training with confidential data.
- Untrusted environments or networks: verifying artifact hashes and
  encrypting data in transit.
- Multi-Tenant environments: tenant isolation, resource allocation,
  model sharing, and hardware (GPU/TPU) side-channel attack awareness.

Why:
- Issue #19213 highlighted that the existing SECURITY.md only covered
  private vulnerability reporting. It lacked guidance on safe usage,
  which left users without clear best practices and caused the project
  to receive false-positive vulnerability reports.
- Providing this guidance benefits both users (who gain concrete
  recommendations for securely running models in their applications)
  and maintainers (who can redirect out-of-scope reports toward the
  documented usage guidance).
- The section explicitly clarifies that the topics under "Using Keras
  Securely" are not considered Keras vulnerabilities, preserving the
  original private-reporting workflow while setting clear expectations
  about what constitutes a real vulnerability.

messages.kimi:
fix: Fix `keras.ops.softmax` error in TensorFlow graph execution (#19299)

Replace `backend.shape(x)` with `x.shape` in the softmax warning check to prevent errors when TensorFlow returns symbolic tensors for unknown shapes during graph execution. The regression was introduced in d5a4521 where using `backend.shape()` triggered an error in TensorFlow's compiled functions.
messages.claude:
fix: replace `backend.shape` with `x.shape` in `keras.ops.softmax` to fix graph execution error

The softmax warning logic used `backend.shape(x)` to check whether the
softmax axis has size 1. Under the TensorFlow backend, `backend.shape`
returns symbolic tensors for inputs with unknown shape (e.g. when used
inside a `keras.Model` compiled graph). Accessing an int index on a
symbolic tensor triggers an error during graph construction, breaking
`keras.ops.softmax` whenever it is used inside a TensorFlow compiled
function (issue #19299).

Switch the check and the warning message to use `x.shape` instead,
which returns a static `None` for unknown dimensions and avoids the
symbolic-tensor indexing error. This restores compatibility with model
graph compilation (e.g. the KerasCV test suite that surfaced the
regression).

Add `test_softmax_in_graph` to cover the scenario by building a model
with a softmax layer over an unknown-shape input and running
`model.predict`, ensuring the graph compiles and executes without
error.
messages.minimax:
Fix `keras.ops.softmax` error when used in TensorFlow compiled functions

When using `keras.ops.softmax` inside a TensorFlow compiled function (e.g., in a Keras Model), the TensorFlow backend's `shape()` returns symbolic tensors which trigger errors during graph execution. This change replaces `backend.shape(x)` with `x.shape` to avoid the symbolic tensor issue. A test case is added to verify softmax works correctly in graph execution contexts.

messages.claude:
fix: Attention compute_output_shape returns value dim instead of query dim (#19257)

The Attention layer's compute_output_shape returned input_shape[0], which is
the query tensor's shape. However, the Attention output's last dimension
follows the value tensor, not the query tensor. This caused model.summary()
to report an incorrect output shape (e.g., (None, 8, 5) instead of the
expected (None, 8, 7)) when query and value had different feature sizes,
which differs from Keras 2 behavior and breaks downstream shape inference.

Fix compute_output_shape to return (*input_shape[0][:-1], input_shape[1][-1]),
preserving the query's sequence length while taking the value's feature
dimension, matching the actual output produced by the call path.

Also remove the dedicated uint8 branch in dtype_policy._parse_name, since the
generic fallback path already handles uint8 via backend.standardize_dtype,
making the special case redundant.

Add a regression test verifying that compute_output_shape matches the real
output shape for query/value/key inputs with differing feature dimensions.
messages.kimi:
fix: Fix Attention layer compute_output_shape to return value tensor dimensions

The Attention layer's compute_output_shape was incorrectly returning the query tensor shape instead of the value tensor shape. According to attention mechanism semantics, the output should have the same dimensions as the value tensor (specifically the last dimension), while maintaining the query tensor's sequence length.

This fix ensures that when query and value tensors have different last dimensions (e.g., query with 5 features and value with 7 features), the output shape correctly reflects the value tensor's feature dimension, matching Keras 2 behavior and user expectations.

Changes:
- Fixed compute_output_shape in Attention layer to return (*query_shape[:-1], value_shape[-1])
- Removed redundant uint8 handling in dtype_policy.py (handled by standardize_dtype)
- Added test case to verify compute_output_shape matches actual output

Fixes #19257
messages.minimax:
Fix Attention compute_output_shape to return value tensor's last dimension

The Attention layer's compute_output_shape was incorrectly returning the query tensor's last dimension instead of the value tensor's last dimension. When query, value, and key have different last dimensions (e.g., query/key with 5 units and value with 7 units), this caused the reported output shape to be wrong, which then cascaded to model.summary() showing incorrect shapes.

The fix ensures compute_output_shape returns (*input_shape[0][:-1], input_shape[1][-1]) so that the reported output shape matches the actual runtime output shape.

messages.kimi:
fix: Fix compute_output_shape in Bidirectional layer to resolve type error (#19328)

The compute_output_shape method was attempting to concatenate lists and tuples, causing a "Can only concatenate list (not 'tuple') to list" error when using Bidirectional LSTM with return_state=True. This occurred because the method was returning inconsistent types - sometimes lists, sometimes tuples - and using copy.copy unnecessarily.

The fix ensures all return values are properly converted to tuples and removes redundant copy operations. This aligns the output shape calculation with expected tuple-based shape conventions in Keras 3, resolving the regression introduced in version 3.1.0.
messages.minimax:
Fix compute_output_shape in Bidirectional layer when merge_mode=None and return_state=True

When merge_mode=None and return_state=True, the compute_output_shape method was returning mixed types (lists and tuples), causing a TypeError when concatenating state_shape (tuple) with output_shape (list). This fix ensures consistent tuple returns for all code paths in compute_output_shape, resolving the "Can only concatenate list (not 'tuple') to list" error.
messages.claude:
fix: return tuples from compute_output_shape in Bidirectional layer

The Bidirectional.compute_output_shape method previously mixed lists and
tuples when assembling the output shape for the merge_mode=None and
return_state=True cases (e.g. `output_shape + state_shape + copy.copy(state_shape)`
where output_shape was a list and state_shape a tuple, and `[output_shape] + state_shape + copy.copy(state_shape)`).

This caused "Can only concatenate list (not 'tuple') to list" errors
when an Embedding layer's output was fed into a Bidirectional LSTM with
return_state=True (issue #19328), a regression observed when moving from
TF/Keras 2.15 to Keras 3.1.

The fix consistently returns tuples across all branches (including the
merge_mode=None case, which now shares a single output_shape reference
instead of a copy, and the plain return path which is wrapped in tuple()),
so callers receive a uniform tuple type regardless of merge_mode or
return_state. The copy.copy calls were unnecessary since the shapes are
only forwarded, not mutated.

A test_output_shape case is added covering all merge modes with and
without return_state to guard against regressions.

messages.kimi:
fix: Fix dtype propagation in random operations for mixed precision compatibility

Fix dtype handling in `keras.random` operations and regularization layers to ensure proper type propagation when using mixed precision (efloat16/bfloat16). 

The changes address issue #19437 where GaussianDropout failed with mixed_bfloat16 due to dtype mismatches in TensorFlow backend operations. The fix ensures:
- Random operations (gamma, binomial, beta) in TensorFlow backend use float32 intermediate dtype for bfloat16 inputs since TF's stateless random ops don't natively support bfloat16
- Dropout operations in NumPy backend preserve input dtype after scaling
- Truncated normal in PyTorch backend correctly uses specified dtype
- GaussianDropout and GaussianNoise layers explicitly pass compute_dtype to random operations
- Test cases updated to properly test training mode behavior

This ensures consistent dtype handling across all backends when using mixed precision policies.
messages.claude:
Fix bfloat16 dtype handling in random ops and dropout layers (#19437)

The `keras.random` backend functions and dropout/noise layers did not
propagate the caller's dtype, defaulting to `floatx()` (float32). Under
a `mixed_bfloat16` policy this produced type mismatches such as
`Input 'y' of 'Mul' Op has type float32 that does not match type
bfloat16 of argument 'x'` from `GaussianDropout.call()` (issue #19437).

- `numpy.random.dropout` now captures `inputs.dtype` and casts the
  scaled keep-prob tensor back to that dtype before `np.where`, since
  dividing a bfloat16 input by a float python scalar upcasts to
  float32.
- `tensorflow.random` `gamma`, `binomial`, and `beta` fall back to an
  float32 intermediate dtype when requested dtype is bfloat16, because
  `tf.random.stateless_gamma`/`stateless_binomial` do not support
  bfloat16, then cast the result back to the requested dtype.
- `torch.random.truncated_normal` now threads the requested dtype
  through the `torch.empty` buffer so the gathered values are not
  silently upcast to float32.
- `GaussianDropout` and `GaussianNoise` pass `self.compute_dtype` to
  the underlying `random.normal` call so the generated noise matches the
  layer's compute dtype under mixed precision.
- Tests for `alpha_dropout`, `dropout`, `gaussian_dropout`, and
  `gaussian_noise` invoke the layers with `training=True` to exercise
  the stochastic path.
- Add `RandomDTypeTest` parameterized over all supported integer and
  float dtypes (including bfloat16) to assert each `keras.random`
  function returns the requested dtype.

This resolves the mixed_bfloat16 regression reported in #19437 and
ensures `keras.random` honors the caller dtype across numpy, tensorflow,
and torch backends.
messages.minimax:
fix random layers to preserve dtype and handle bfloat16 limitations

The issue stems from GaussianDropout (and other regularization layers) not passing dtype to backend random functions, causing dtype mismatches with bfloat16. The TF backend's stateless_gamma and stateless_binomial don't support bfloat16, requiring float32 as intermediate dtype with explicit casting. Regularization layers now pass compute_dtype to backend functions, and numpy/tensorflow backends ensure proper dtype preservation in dropout and other random operations.

context.issue:
Issue #19152: Change keras.Model inheritance for improved static analysis support
Hi all,

The `keras.Model` class may inherit from one of many different trainer classes. This is chosen at runtime by a conditional statement, which makes static analysis difficult. 

Knowing Python's Method Resolution Order (MRO) and the fact that all trainer classes have a common base class, I propose that `keras.Model` should inherit from the base trainer class. The change is minimal and would look like this:

```python
class Model(Trainer, Layer, base_trainer.Trainer):
```

This change fixes the syntax highlighting in my IDE, so I would really appreciate it.

Also, I believe it would also make the direct assignment of docstrings unnecessary, as they would be inherited from the base trainer class. The current state of the code is as follows:

```python
Model.fit.__doc__ = base_trainer.Trainer.fit.__doc__
Model.predict.__doc__ = base_trainer.Trainer.predict.__doc__
...
```

Thank you for your time and consideration.

messages.kimi:
fix: fix Model class inheritance for improved static analysis and type checking (#19152)

The `keras.Model` class now explicitly inherits from `base_trainer.Trainer` in addition to `Trainer` and `Layer`. This change enables proper static analysis by IDEs and type checkers, as the runtime conditional inheritance made type inference difficult.

Additionally, this change allows removal of the manual docstring assignments (e.g., `Model.fit.__doc__ = base_trainer.Trainer.fit.__doc__`) since methods now properly inherit documentation through the MRO.

Added `__new__` methods with `typing.cast()` to `Functional` and `Sequential` classes to ensure proper type annotations are preserved when these classes are instantiated.
messages.claude:
refactor: change Model inheritance to base trainer for static analysis support

The `keras.Model` class dynamically inherits from one of several trainer
classes selected at runtime via a conditional statement. This runtime
selection makes static analysis difficult, breaking IDE features like
syntax highlighting and type inference (issue #19152).

To resolve this, `Model` now also inherits from `base_trainer.Trainer`
directly. Since all runtime-selected trainer classes share this common
base, the MRO is preserved and runtime behavior is unchanged, while
static analyzers can now resolve the trainer methods on `Model`.

Additionally, the manual docstring assignments previously needed to
expose trainer docs on `Model` (`Model.fit.__doc__ = ...`, etc.) are now
redundant because the docs are inherited via the new base class link, so
they have been removed.

Finally, `typing.cast` is added to `__new__` in `Model`, `Functional`,
and `Sequential`. Because `__new__` returns an instance created by a
parent `__new__`, static type checkers cannot infer the correct return
type (they would see the parent type rather than the subclass). The
`typing.cast` calls allow these classes — including `Functional` and
`Sequential`, which can now be used as submodels — to be properly typed
when instantiated, complementing the static analysis improvements.
messages.minimax:
fix: resolve type annotation issues with Model subclassing

The Model class inheritance structure made static analysis difficult because the trainer base was conditionally selected at runtime. This change explicitly adds `base_trainer.Trainer` to the Model inheritance and uses `typing.cast` in `__new__` methods to ensure proper type inference when subclassing Functional and Sequential models. The manual docstring assignments for fit/predict/evaluate methods are removed since they are now inherited from the base trainer class.

In Keras 3.2.1 the imdb.load_data function returns a Python list instead of a ndarray object as described in the function documentation. 
In Keras 2.15 the train and test data are converted to a ndarray using the following statements before returning the tuple.

Torch 2.3.0 introduces a breaking change that causes AttributeError: 'Parameter' object has no attribute 'fget' when running matmul operations with Keras variables. messages.minimax: pin torch < 2.3.0 to fix AttributeError on Parameter object (#19602)
messages.claude:
build: pin torch < 2.3.0 to fix torch CPU test failures

Torch 2.3.0 (currently available via the PyTorch download wheels but not
yet on PyPI) breaks our torch backend tests. `ops.matmul` ends up calling
into `backend/torch/numpy.py`, where `Parameter` objects no longer expose
an `fget` attribute, raising `AttributeError: 'Parameter' object has no
attribute 'fget'` and failing tests such as `TestTrainer.test_fit_flow_jit`
(see CI log: https://github.com/keras-team/keras/actions/runs/8804994492/job/24166626153).

Since we pull torch wheels directly from the PyTorch downloads folder,
2.3.0 gets picked up ahead of an official PyPI release, so cap torch at
`>=2.1.0, <2.3.0` across `requirements.txt`,
`requirements-jax-cuda.txt`, and `requirements-tensorflow-cuda.txt` to
keep CI green until the upstream regression is addressed (GitHub issue

messages.kimi:
fix: Fix shape mismatch in LayerNormalization with rms_scaling and multi-axis

Fix a bug where `self.gamma` was not properly broadcast when using `rms_scaling=True` with multiple axes (e.g., `axis=[-3, -2]`). The gamma tensor shape did not match the broadcasted input shape, causing an "Incompatible shapes" error during multiplication. messages.claude:
fix: broadcast gamma in layernorm rms_scaling path

When rms_scaling=True, gamma was not broadcast to match the input shape,
causing "Incompatible shapes" errors when normalizing along non-final axes
(e.g. axis=[-3, -2]). The gamma tensor retains its original (non-broadcast)
shape while `inputs * inv` is already broadcast to the full input shape, so
the multiplication fails.

Apply `_broadcast(self.gamma)` before casting so gamma is reshaped to align
with the reduction axis, mirroring the broadcast already used in the
non-rms_scaling branch. Fixes #19642.
messages.minimax:
Fix bug in LayerNormalization with rms_scaling=True and multiple axes

When using `rms_scaling=True` with multiple normalization axes (e.g., `axis=[-3, -2]`), the gamma parameter was not being broadcast to the correct shape before multiplication with inputs, causing an incompatible shapes error (e.g., `[1,1920,1200,3]` vs `[1920,1200]`). This change wraps gamma with `_broadcast(self.gamma)` to ensure proper broadcasting behavior matching the input tensor shape.

messages.kimi:
feat: Add `name` parameter to MobileNetV3 to enable multiple instances in one model

Add a `name` parameter to MobileNetV3, MobileNetV3Small, and MobileNetV3Large functions, allowing users to specify custom model names. This fixes the ValueError that occurred when trying to use multiple MobileNetV3 instances as sub-modules in the same model, as Keras requires unique operation names. Default names are preserved for backward compatibility: "MobileNetV3Small" and "MobileNetV3Large" for the respective variants.
messages.claude:
feat: Add `name` arg to MobileNetV3 to support multiple instances in one model

Adds a `name` parameter to `MobileNetV3` (and its `MobileNetV3Small`/
`MobileNetV3Large` wrappers) so callers can supply a custom model name
instead of always getting the hard-coded `"MobilenetV3" + model_type`.

Why: Previously the model name was hard-coded inside `MobileNetV3`, so
creating two instances of MobileNetV3 as sub-modules of a larger model
failed with `ValueError: The name "MobilenetV3small" is used 2 times in
the model. All operation names should be unique.` Keras does not auto-
resolve name collisions across sub-models, and there was no way to pass
a distinct name through the `applications` API. The new `name` arg lets
users disambiguate instances, while the `Small`/`Large` helpers default

messages.kimi:
fix(ops): handle array-like repeats and improve error messages in keras.ops.repeat (#19826)

Fix `keras.ops.repeat` to properly handle array-like `repeats` argument when computing output shape for `KerasTensor` inputs. Previously, when `axis=None` and `repeats` was a list/array, the output shape calculation was incorrect because it didn't account for broadcasting rules properly.

The fix:
- Normalizes `repeats` to a list early in `compute_output_spec`
- Adds proper broadcasting support when `repeats` has size 1
- Adds validation to ensure `repeats` size matches the flattened tensor size when not broadcasting
- Returns dynamic shape (None) when axis dimension is unknown
- Improves error messages for dimension mismatches

This ensures consistent behavior between symbolic tensors (`KerasTensor`) and concrete tensors, aligning with NumPy's repeat semantics.
messages.claude:
fix: `keras.ops.repeat` cannot return expected shape when `x` is a `KerasTensor` and `axis` is `None`

When `x` is a symbolic `KerasTensor` and `repeats` is a list/array, `compute_output_spec`
incorrectly broadcast the single-element list `[N]` as if it were an int scalar `N`, producing
the wrong output shape (e.g. `(784,)` instead of `(501760,)` in issue #19821). The root cause was
that `isinstance(self.repeats, int)` did not account for the broadcast case where `repeats` is a
1-element sequence and should be broadcast against the flattened input.

This change reworks `Repeat.compute_output_spec` to:
- Treat a 1-element `repeats` sequence as a broadcast (matching NumPy semantics) by multiplying the
  flattened/input-axis size by `repeats[0]`.
- Validate that a multi-element `repeats` has compatible size with the flattened input (axis=None)
  or the specified axis, raising a clear `ValueError` with the received sizes when they mismatch.
- Preserve dynamic shape semantics: when the size on `axis` is `None` (unknown), keep the output
  dimension dynamic instead of falling through the int path and erroring.
- Fix the symbolic test that expected `(3, 3)` for `knp.repeat(x, [1, 2], axis=0)` on a dynamic
  axis-0 input, which should actually be `(None, 3)`.

Adds unit tests covering the broadcast case (`repeats=[2]`), the new `ValueError` paths for
incompatible sizes, dynamic-axis behavior, and a backend test exercising `np.ndarray` repeats
(`knp.Repeat(np.array([2]))`) against the NumPy reference.

Refs #19821.
messages.minimax:
fix(ops): Fix `keras.ops.repeat` compute_output_spec for KerasTensor with axis=None

When `x` is a `KerasTensor` and `axis` is `None`, `compute_output_spec` incorrectly calculated the output shape when `repeats` was a list. The old code computed `sum(repeats)` as the output size after flattening, but it should broadcast a single-element repeats list (like NumPy) or validate that the repeats size matches the flattened dimension size.

Also fixes an incorrect test assertion where `knp.repeat(x, [1, 2], axis=0)` with `x.shape=(None, 3)` incorrectly expected shape `(3, 3)` instead of `(None, 3)`.

messages.kimi:
fix: Add validation for mask dimension in BatchNormalization

Add a check in `BatchNormalization.call()` to ensure the mask has exactly one less dimension than the inputs. This prevents cryptic shape mismatch errors during the broadcast multiplication operation when users provide an incorrectly shaped mask. The validation raises a clear `ValueError` with shape information to help users debug the issue.
messages.claude:
fix: validate mask shape in BatchNormalization.call

Add an explicit shape check at the start of BatchNormalization.call that
raises a ValueError when the mask's rank is not exactly one less than the
inputs' rank.

Why: When a caller passed a mask whose rank mismatched the inputs (e.g. a
mask of shape (1, 2) against inputs of shape (1, 2, 3, 4)), the layer
previously proceeded with the incompatible mask and failed deep inside
the backend with an opaque InvalidArgumentError
("Incompatible shapes: [1,2,1] vs. [1,2,3,4] [Op:Mul]") that gave no
indication of the root cause (issue #19818).

Validating the mask shape up front produces a clear, actionable error
message referencing both mask.shape and inputs.shape, so users can
diagnose and correct the mask dimensions immediately instead of debugging
through the underlying op failure. This mirrors the descriptive error
pattern introduced for the same layer in #19829.
messages.minimax:
Add mask dimension validation to BatchNormalization.call()

Raise a clear ValueError when the mask does not have exactly one less dimension than the inputs, instead of letting an incompatible shapes error occur deep in the computation. Fixes the confusing error when using masked BatchNormalization with inputs of more than 3 dimensions.

messages.kimi:
fix(losses): fix sparse_categorical_crossentropy with ignore_class for 4D inputs (#19838)

* Fix `sparse_categorical_crossentropy` failing when `ignore_class` is used with 4D inputs that have a trailing dimension of 1 in y_true

* Add squeeze operation to remove trailing dimension when y_true has shape (..., 1) matching y_pred's rank

* Update tests to handle the fixed behavior and improve precision

The issue was that when y_true has shape (Batch x Height x Width x 1) and y_pred has shape (Batch x Height x Width x Class), the function incorrectly expanded dimensions, causing a shape mismatch. The fix automatically squeezes the trailing dimension from y_true when it equals 1, aligning with expected behavior for semantic segmentation and similar use cases.
messages.claude:
fix(losses): handle 4D inputs in `sparse_categorical_crossentropy` with `ignore_class`

When `y_true` had a trailing singleton dimension (e.g. shape (batch, height, width, 1)) while `y_pred` was expanded to (batch, height, width, num_classes), the shapes mismatched and `ignore_class` raised a ValueError on 4D inputs (issue #19825).

Squeeze the last axis of `y_true` when it equals 1 and the tensor ranks already match `y_pred`, so the `ignore_class` masking path receives consistent shapes regardless of input rank.

Update tests to cover the 4D `(batch, h, w, 1)` case and relax the `assertAllClose` precision argument where full precision is now expected.

messages.kimi:
fix: Replace import * with explicit imports in toplevel __init__.py

The use of `from keras.api import *` in the toplevel `__init__.py` breaks
static type checking, as type checkers cannot resolve dynamically imported
symbols. This causes IDE errors when importing keras submodules like
`keras.models`.

Replace the wildcard import with explicit imports of all API symbols.
Update `api_gen.py` to auto-generate these explicit imports by inspecting
the `keras.api` module at build time, rather than hardcoding them as a
string template. This makes the `__init__.py` file the source of truth
while keeping the import section auto-generated.

Fixes #19779
messages.claude:
fix: stop using `import *` in toplevel keras init (#19864)

Replace `from keras.api import *` in `keras/__init__.py` with explicit
per-symbol imports generated by `api_gen.py`, so static type checkers
can resolve symbols imported from `keras.api`.

Why: issue #19779 reports that the dynamic `__path__.append` + `import *`
approach introduced in 04891e89da is opaque to static type checkers
(e.g. VS Code/Pylance), causing `import keras.models` to surface errors
in 3.3.1 that did not occur in 3.2.1. `import *` also breaks type
inference for the `keras` namespace.

Changes:
- `api_gen.py`: `update_package_init` now reads the in-repo
  `keras/__init__.py` (template) and writes the build copy, emitting an
  explicit `from keras.api import <symbol>` line for every public symbol
  in `keras.api` between the `# DO NOT EDIT.` / `# END DO NOT EDIT.`
  markers. The previous approach inlined the entire init file as a
  Python string, which was clunky and unreadable.
- Introduce `BUILD_DIR_NAME = "tmp_build_dir"` constant to avoid
  scattering the magic string.
- Import the built `api` module via `importlib.import_module` so the
  generator enumerates the actual exported symbols rather than relying
  on `import *` semantics.
- `keras/__init__.py` is now the source of truth in the repo, with
  only the import block auto-regenerated, instead of being fully
  autogenerated and stored as a string inside `api_gen.py`.

Fixes #19779
messages.minimax:
fix api_gen.py: generate explicit imports instead of import * to fix typechecking

The dynamic `import *` and `__path__.append` approach in keras/__init__.py breaks static type checking (issue #19779). Instead of using string replacement to inject imports, the update_package_init function now uses a template-based approach with importlib to dynamically import all symbols from keras.api and generate explicit import statements. This allows type checkers like pyright to properly resolve symbol definitions.

messages.kimi:
fix: Fix import error for private `_tf_keras` symbol in keras __init__.py (#19875)

The change fixes an ImportError where `_tf_keras` cannot be imported from `keras.api`. The root cause was in `api_gen.py` where the filter logic for determining which symbols to import was incorrect - it was checking for double underscore prefix (`__`) instead of single underscore (`_`), causing private symbols like `_tf_keras` to be incorrectly included in the generated imports.

The fix updates the filter condition from `symbol.startswith("__")` to `symbol.startswith("_")` to properly exclude all private symbols (single underscore) while still allowing `__version__` to be imported. This aligns with the intended behavior of only importing public symbols from the API module.

Fixes #19875
messages.claude:
fix: stop exporting private `_tf_keras` symbol from keras.api

The api_gen.py script was generating `from keras.api import _tf_keras`
in keras/__init__.py, but `_tf_keras` is a private symbol (single
underscore) that is not part of the public API surface and is not
guaranteed to exist in keras.api. This caused an ImportError at
`import keras` time for users of keras-nightly:

    ImportError: cannot import name '_tf_keras' from 'keras.api'

The root cause is in update_package_init: the symbol filter only
excluded dunders (`__` prefix) while still re-exporting all single-
underscore private symbols. Tighten the filter to skip any symbol
starting with `_` (except `__version__`, which is intentionally
public), so generated __init__.py files only import truly public
symbols and no longer depend on internal implementation details.

Fixes #19875
messages.minimax:
Remove import of private `_tf_keras` symbol from keras namespace

The `_tf_keras` symbol is a private implementation detail and should not be exposed in the public keras namespace. Issue #19875 shows that users encountered `ImportError: cannot import name '_tf_keras' from 'keras.api'` because this private symbol was being imported at the top level but wasn't actually available in the keras.api module. This commit removes that explicit import and corrects the symbol filtering logic in api_gen.py to properly exclude single-underscore private symbols while still allowing dunder symbols like `__version__` through.

messages.kimi:
fix: Move data batch fetching to only when model/metrics need building

The _symbolic_build method was fetching a data batch from the iterator
whenever the model, compile metrics, OR optimizer was unbuilt. However,
the data batch is only needed for building the model and compile metrics,
not for the optimizer. This caused issues with custom Python generators
on the Torch backend, where unnecessary iteration could lead to
UnboundLocalError when the training loop was skipped.

By moving the data batch fetching logic inside the model/metrics build
condition, we avoid consuming data from the iterator when only the
optimizer needs to be built. This fixes the training failure with
custom generators reported in issue #19929.
messages.claude:
fix: resolve data_batch fetch placement in `_symbolic_build` for torch custom generators (#19929)

Move the iterator fallback that populates `data_batch` inside the
`model_unbuilt or compile_metrics_unbuilt` branch in
`Trainer._symbolic_build`. Previously the fallback ran in a separate
outer `if` block that also covered `optimizer_unbuilt`, so when only the
optimizer needed building, the code consumed the first batch from the
iterator (via `enumerate_epoch`) but never used it, advancing the
generator past its first batch.

For the torch backend, where generators are not rewindable and
`enumerate_epoch` wraps the user-provided generator directly, consuming
the first batch at build time meant it was missing when the actual
training loop ran. This caused the training loop to be skipped entirely,
surfacing as `UnboundLocalError: local variable 'logs' referenced before
assignment` (reported in #19929), since `logs` is only assigned inside
the per-batch loop body that never executed.

By relocating the fallback to only run when symbolic inputs are
actually required (model or metrics unbuilt), the torch iterator is no
longer drained during optimizer-only builds, allowing custom Python
generators to be trained successfully on the torch backend while keeping
the TF/JAX paths unchanged.

messages.kimi:
feat: Add `__int__`, `__float__`, and `__round__` methods to KerasVariable for Python scalar conversion

Add `__int__` and `__float__` methods to `KerasVariable` to enable Python scalar conversion for scalar arrays, with proper error handling for non-scalar arrays. Also add `__round__` method to support the built-in `round()` function. Refactor all comparison and arithmetic magic methods to use backend numpy operations for consistent dtype handling across backends. Add `__int__` and `__float__` to `KerasTensor` with clear error messages explaining that symbolic tensors cannot be converted to Python scalars.

This fixes the issue where users couldn't retrieve learning rate values from Keras Variables and where `round()` failed on Variables as reported in #19952.
messages.claude:
fix: enable `KerasVariable` and `KerasTensor` scalar conversions and operator dispatch via backend numpy ops

What:
- Add `__int__`, `__float__`, and `__round__` to `KerasTensor` (raises on symbolic tensors) and `KerasVariable` (scalar-only conversion with shape guard).
- Rewrite all binary/arithmetic/comparison dunders on `KerasVariable` to delegate to `backend.numpy.*` instead of the per-backend `value.__op__` + `_convert_to_tensor` path.
- Route `Variable` through multiple inheritance of `BackendVariable` and `KerasVariable` so the shared dunders apply across TF/JAX/Torch.
- Move the `isinstance(x, Variable)` short-circuit in torch `convert_to_tensor` to a `type(x) is Variable` check to avoid TorchDynamo errors.
- Update `seed_generator.next` to use `backend.numpy.add` for state increment.
- Restructure `variables_test.py` into correctness/behavior/dtype suites; add JAX-parity dtype tests for every operator.

Why:
- Issue #19952: users cannot read a learning-rate `Variable` as a Python scalar, and `round(variable)` raises `TypeError: type Variable doesn't define __round__ method`. Keras 3 dropped `tf.keras.backend.get_value`, so `Variable` must support `int()`, `float()`, and `round()` directly.
- The old `value.__add__(self._convert_to_tensor(other, dtype=value.dtype))` implementation produced backend-specific (and often wrong) result dtypes — e.g. JAX weak type promotion on `uint64`, and inconsistent `bool`/`int8` outputs for comparisons. Routing through `backend.numpy.{equal,less,add,...}` aligns Keras dtype behavior with JAX, which is now the reference in the new `VariableOpsDTypeTest` suite.
- `KerasTensor` previously lacked `__int__`/`__float__`/`__round__`, so symbolic tensors silently fell through to NumPy's `__array__` and gave misleading errors; the new overrides surface an explicit message consistent with the existing `__array__` guard.
- The torch `convert_to_tensor` `isinstance` check broke under `TorchDynamo` (`GetAttrVariable has no type`); switching to `type(x) is Variable` preserves the fast path without the dynamo failure, matching the comment already in the code.
messages.minimax:
feat: Add `__int__`, `__float__`, `__round__` and fix dtype consistency for `Variable` and `KerasTensor`

Why:
- Issue #19952: Users cannot extract scalar values from KerasVariable (e.g., learning rate) via `int()`, `float()`, or `round()` because these methods were missing.
- The documentation example for `LearningRateScheduler` fails with `TypeError: type Variable doesn't define __round__ method`.
- Existing comparison and arithmetic operators on KerasVariable used direct value operations, which bypass backend dtype promotion rules and cause inconsistent behavior across backends (JAX, PyTorch, TensorFlow).
- The torch backend had a bug where `isinstance(x, Variable)` check fails under TorchDynamo, causing incorrect tensor conversion.

How:
- Add `__int__` and `__float__` to KerasVariable (with shape validation) and KerasTensor (raises descriptive error since symbolic tensors have no value).
- Add `__round__` to both KerasVariable and KerasTensor using the corresponding backend ops.
- Refactor all comparison and arithmetic dunder methods on KerasVariable to route through `backend.numpy.*` functions, ensuring consistent dtype promotion matching JAX behavior.
- Fix torch conversion by using `type(x) is Variable` instead of `isinstance`.
- Fix seed_generator to use `backend.numpy.add` for consistency.

messages.kimi:
fix: Add consistent shape validation in MultiHeadAttention build method

Add validation checks in the build method to ensure query_shape[-1] equals value_shape[-1] and value_shape[1:-1] equals key_shape[1:-1]. This fixes inconsistent assertion behavior where shape mismatches were only caught when using Keras tensors but not with torch tensors. The validation now runs consistently regardless of input type, preventing silent errors and providing clear error messages for incompatible shapes. Fixes #19769.
messages.claude:
fix: validate query/value and value/key shape compatibility in MHA build

Adds explicit shape validation in MultiHeadAttention.build() to catch
mismatches between query, value, and key tensors early. Previously, the
shape assertion was only triggered in certain code paths (e.g. when
using Keras tensors with dynamic batch shapes), while passing torch
tensors with static batch shapes silently bypassed it. This led to
inconsistent behavior where invalid configurations went undetected
depending on the backend and input type, as reported in #19769.

Two checks are now enforced:
- The last dimension of query_shape and value_shape must be equal.
- All non-last dimensions of value_shape and key_shape must be equal.

The existing test_shape_mismatch_error case is extended to also verify
that calling the layer with mismatched inputs raises the error at
runtime, not only during compute_output_shape.

Fixes #19769
messages.minimax:
fix: Add shape validation in MultiHeadAttention.build() for query/value/key

Fixes inconsistent assertion behavior where shape mismatches between query and value were only sometimes caught depending on the backend used.

Previously, mismatched last dimensions of query and value (e.g., query_shape[-1]=16 vs value_shape[-1]=8) would not raise an error in some backends (e.g., torch), while the Keras Input layer path would raise ValueError. This change adds explicit validation in build() to ensure consistent error handling regardless of backend.

Also validates that all dimensions of value and key (except the last) are equal.

Fixes #19769

messages.kimi:
feat: Extend Sequential._maybe_rebuild to support functional/sequential models as first layer

Enable Sequential models to automatically build when the first layer is a Functional or Sequential model that has an `input_shape` property. This fixes the "Undefined shapes are not supported" error when using nested models.

Previously, `_maybe_rebuild` only checked for `InputLayer` instances to determine if the model could be built. This change adds support for layers that have an `input_shape` attribute (commonly Functional models), allowing Sequential models to properly initialize when composed of other models as the first layer. Also updates `summary_utils.py` to use `output_shape` property when available, avoiding unnecessary `compute_output_shape` calls that could fail on nested models.
messages.minimax:
Fix Sequential model build and `.summary()` when using functional/sequential submodel as first layer

When a Functional model or nested Sequential model is used as the first layer of a Sequential model, `_maybe_rebuild` could not determine the input shape since it only checked for `InputLayer`. This caused a "ValueError: Undefined shapes are not supported" error during build and `.summary()` calls. The fix adds handling for layers with an `input_shape` property (found in Functional models) and updates `format_shape` to handle layers that have `output_shape` directly rather than requiring `compute_output_shape`.
messages.claude:
feat: Enable Sequential model to build when a Functional/Sequential model is the first layer

What:
- Extend `Sequential._maybe_rebuild` to detect when the first layer exposes an `input_shape` property (i.e. a Functional or nested Sequential model) and use it to build the parent Sequential.
- Update `summary_utils.format_shape_summary` to prefer `layer.output_shape` when available, falling back to `compute_output_shape` only otherwise, so the summary path no longer requires `_build_shapes_dict` on model-typed layers.

Why:
Issue #19982 reports `ValueError: Undefined shapes are not supported.` when calling `model.summary()` on a model that nests another Functional/Sequential model (e.g. a Siamese network whose embedding sub-model is a `keras.Model`). The root cause is that `Sequential._maybe_rebuild` only handled the `InputLayer` case, so a Sequential whose first layer is a Functional/Sequential sub-model was never rebuilt and thus never had its sub-layer shapes propagated upward. The matching `summary_utils` path then tried to read `_build_shapes_dict`, which is absent on model-typed layers, raising the `ValueError`.

This change lets a Functional or Sequential model serve as the first layer of a Sequential model (and as a sub-model in general), matching the behavior described in the issue and unblocking Siamese-style architectures. Tests cover both Functional and Sequential first-layer scenarios, including eager and symbolic calls and `model.summary()`.

messages.claude:
fix: regression in 3D convolution with channels_first on GPU

The previous workaround for broken CPU ops used `inputs.device.split(":")[-2]`
to detect CPU placement, which fails for symbolic tensors (e.g. when
`run_eagerly=False`) because the device string is empty, causing an
IndexError during graph tracing (issue #19991).

Restructure the conv path to route all cases that need XLA through a
single `_conv_xla()` helper, keyed on a `needs_xla` flag that covers both
grouped convolutions and channels_first 3D convolutions. This avoids
inspecting `inputs.device` entirely, so symbolic tensors no longer
trigger the crash, while still working around the underlying TF CPU bugs.

Add a tracing test (`tf.function` wrapping `knn.conv`) to guard against
future regressions of this kind.
messages.kimi:
fix: Fix IndexError in 3D convolution with channels_first on GPU (#19991)

The previous implementation attempted to check if the tensor was on CPU by parsing `inputs.device`, which fails for symbolic tensors when `run_eagerly=False`. This caused an IndexError when using Conv3D with channels_first data format on GPU.

The fix refactors the XLA compilation logic to use a declarative approach: instead of checking the device at runtime, we now determine XLA necessity based on known-broken operation patterns (channels_first 3D convolutions and grouped convolutions on CPU). This eliminates the problematic device string parsing while maintaining the same workarounds for TensorFlow CPU limitations.
messages.minimax:
Fix #19991: Conv3D channels_first regression on GPU with run_eagerly=False

TensorFlow's Conv3D with channels_first data format is broken on CPU when not
running eagerly. The previous code used `inputs.device.split(":")[-2]` to check
device type, which fails for symbolic tensors (causing IndexError: list index out
of range). Instead, always use XLA compilation for channels_first 3D convolutions
and grouped convolutions to work around TensorFlow's CPU limitations.
